Problem: The paper studies temporal decay of co-citation predictability in legal statutes over time. It constructs a benchmark to measure how retrieval performance degrades over years.

Method: They construct annual snapshots of Ukrainian court decisions, build co-citation matrices, and evaluate leave-one-out citation prediction using graph-based metrics (Adamic-Adar, Common Neighbors, etc.) and a BM25 baseline. They analyze decay across article frequency bands and legal domains.

Key assumptions: maybe that co-citation structure reflects retrieval signal; that leave-one-out citation prediction is a proxy for retrieval; that temporal split reflects real-world shift.

Main contribution: A 20-year statute retrieval benchmark with 396M citations, showing significant temporal decay of co-citation predictability, analysis of non-uniform decay, embedding drift analysis, and release of benchmark.

Datasets: UA-StatuteRetrieval (Ukrainian court decisions 2007-2026, 101M decisions, 396M citations).

Benchmarks: They evaluate on their own benchmark; they might compare to existing legal retrieval benchmarks like BSARD, SCALE, LeSICiN (mentioned in related work). We'll list those as benchmarks they reference.

Baselines: Adamic-Adar, Common Neighbors, Degree, Random, BM25.

Metrics: MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank), Hit@k (Hit@1,5,10,20).

Results: Adamic-Adar MRR declines 33% on fixed set, 47% under train/test split; BM25 decays 31%; civil law degrades from 0.35 to 0.15; criminal procedure stable; hub articles stable; mid-frequency lose half predictability.

Limitations: The evaluation is a proxy (citation prediction) not end-user QA; focuses on co-citation only; maybe limited to Ukrainian law; etc.

Future work: Extend to other jurisdictions, incorporate text-based methods, study impact on end-to-end QA, etc.

Code availability: Not mentioned; maybe code not released; we can say "not stated in abstract" or check if there is a code URL. The paper metadata shows code_urls empty. We'll say "No code availability stated".

Analyzed_from: we used full text (we fetched text and searched). So analyzed_from="full_text".

Relation_to_idea: We need to compute overlap scores (problem/method/evaluation overlap) and conceptual difference. We'll approximate.

Problem overlap: Both deal with temporal degradation in legal document retrieval. The paper's problem is measuring decay of co-citation signal; our problem is QA reliability dropping due to overlapping revisions. Overlap high: maybe 0.6.

Method overlap: The paper does not propose a temporal weighting framework; it analyzes decay and proposes benchmark. Our method adds temporal relevance component to retriever. Some overlap in using temporal analysis, but different focus. Method overlap maybe 0.3.

Evaluation overlap: They evaluate using citation prediction metrics (MRR, Hit@k). We propose to evaluate using QA metrics (EM, F1). Some overlap in using retrieval metrics but different task. Evaluation overlap maybe 0.2.

Conceptual difference: They focus on measuring stability of co-citation signal as a proxy for retrieval; we focus on improving retrieval for time-specific QA by adding temporal relevance weighting. So difference: they diagnose decay; we propose a mitigation.
